slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 8: Reusing Behavior Through Inheritance. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

Learners should be able to say what Reusing Behavior Through Inheritance changes about program design, not merely identify a keyword. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 8, treat 8.1.2 Controlling Member Accessibility as a design decision with costs and evidence. Public, protected, and private access determine which code can name members through the relevant language rules. The scale is protected in this teaching example so the derived sensor can use it directly. That choice visibly couples the derived class to the base representation. In a production design, a protected query or composed calibration object may preserve more freedom than a protected writable field. Derived code should not casually bypass an invariant established by the base. Private inheritance and protected inheritance have different interface implications; they are not needed merely to demonstrate basic specialization here. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 8, treat 8.2.2 Derived-Class Destruction Order as a design decision with costs and evidence. When the local sensor leaves scope, its derived destructor body runs first, followed by its member and base destruction in the required order. The log records derived destruction and then base destruction. The base in this example is non-polymorphic and has no virtual destructor. Deleting a derived object through an owning base pointer would be invalid for this design, so the example never does that. The expected sequence is base constructed, derived constructed, derived destroyed, base destroyed. The test checks all four events after the sensor has left scope. The source’s reserve call is relevant to cleanup safety: pushing into an already sufficient vector of string views avoids a new allocation for these events. General destructor logging through arbitrary strings or I/O could fail and needs a different policy. This teaching instrument is intentionally bounded. slides.title: Failure clinic — The initializer list that looked ordered
keyPoints: A class lists one member before another in its initializer list, but declares them in the opposite order.
The programmer assumes the visual list controls initialization and reads a member that has not yet been.
A warning can reveal the mismatch, but the durable repair is to arrange declarations and dependencies.
Another defect stores a reference to a temporary observer in a base.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 8, treat Failure clinic — The initializer list that looked ordered as a design decision with costs and evidence. A class lists one member before another in its initializer list, but declares them in the opposite order. The programmer assumes the visual list controls initialization and reads a member that has not yet been initialized. A warning can reveal the mismatch, but the durable repair is to arrange declarations and dependencies intentionally, then write the initializer list in that same order for clarity. Another defect stores a reference to a temporary observer in a base. The sensor’s own scope looks correct, but its cleanup log is already dead. The right question is not “does the sensor still exist?” but “does every borrowed dependency used during its lifetime still exist?” Composition and inheritance both create such dependencies. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

Bases are initialized before the derived portion is ready, and base destruction follows the derived destructor body. Member declaration order also matters regardless of initializer-list presentation.
